blocks.text: 1. Forward Propagation

blocks.alt: Input flows layer by layer into the output

blocks.text: Weights and Biases, the previous topic, covered what a network actually learns during training. Forward Propagation is the process of actually using those learned values to produce a prediction, the computation that turns a raw input into a real, usable output.

Data flows forward through a network, layer by layer, starting at the input and moving all the way through to the output, exactly the sequence already introduced across the earlier Input Layer, Hidden Layer, and Output Layer topics, now covered here as one complete, connected process.
2. The Full Flow

blocks.alt: The input layer feeds hidden layers, which feed the output layer

blocks.text: The full forward propagation flow starts when raw input enters the input layer, which, as already covered in its own topic, performs no computation and simply passes the data onward. Each subsequent layer then computes its own weighted sum plus bias, followed by its activation function.

This continues through every hidden layer in the network, one after another, until the output layer finally produces the network's actual final prediction, the exact output already covered in genuine depth in the Output Layer topic.

blocks.text: 3. One Layer's Computation, in Detail

blocks.alt: The previous layer's output feeds a weighted sum, then an activation

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the layer-as-matrix-operation already covered in the Layers topic. Each individual layer takes the previous layer's output as its own input, multiplies it by this layer's own weight matrix, and adds this layer's own bias vector.

The result then passes through this layer's activation function, and this final, activated result becomes the input to whichever layer comes directly next in the network. Repeating this exact sequence across every layer is, in full, what forward propagation actually is.
4. Why It Is Called Forward

blocks.alt: Input flows in one direction only toward the output

blocks.text: It is called forward propagation because information flows in exactly one direction during this specific step: from the input toward the output, never backward, at any point during this particular computation.

This connects forward to Backpropagation, covered in its own full dedicated module later in this course, which instead flows information backward through the network, computing exactly how each weight and bias should be adjusted. Forward and backward propagation are genuinely two separate, distinct steps, covered separately for exactly this reason.
5. Two Genuinely Different Contexts

blocks.alt: Forward propagation during training is compared against during inference

blocks.text: Forward propagation happens in two genuinely different contexts. During training, it gets followed immediately by a backward pass, using the forward pass's prediction and the resulting error to update the network's weights and biases.

During inference, meaning actually using an already-trained model to make a real prediction, forward propagation happens alone, with no backward pass at all, since the weights and biases are already fixed and are not being further adjusted at that point.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This distinction directly echoes Real-Time Prediction, already covered in the traditional Machine Learning course, where a deployed model runs forward propagation alone, repeatedly, on new incoming data, with no further training happening in that moment.

blocks.text: 6. The Computational Cost

This connects back to the matrix multiplication already covered in both the Layers and Neurons topics. Forward propagation's computational cost is dominated by these matrix multiplications, one per layer, computed in sequence across the entire network.

A wider layer, or a deeper network with more layers overall, directly means more computation required per single forward pass, a genuinely practical consideration covered in further depth in the Production Deep Learning module later in this course, where inference speed becomes a real, concrete deployment concern.
7. Batched Forward Propagation

blocks.alt: A single example expands into a batch, all processed at once

blocks.text: This connects back to the batch dimension already covered in the Input Layer topic. Forward propagation processes an entire batch of examples at once in practice, using the exact same matrix operations already covered in this topic, just with an extra batch dimension added on top.

This is considerably more efficient than looping over each individual example one at a time, exactly why batching, already covered in The Deep Learning Workflow topic, genuinely matters for practical, real-world training and inference speed.
8. Saving Intermediate Values

blocks.alt: Intermediate activations get saved for backpropagation

blocks.text: A genuinely important practical detail is that each layer's output, computed during the forward pass, often gets saved rather than discarded immediately after use. These saved values are needed later for the backward pass, covered in the Backpropagation and Optimization module later in this course.

Discarding these intermediate values immediately would save memory during the forward pass itself, but it would force recomputing them again during backpropagation, a real, deliberate tradeoff between memory usage and computation time that real Deep Learning frameworks actively manage.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: This memory-versus-computation tradeoff becomes a genuinely significant, practical concern for very large, deep networks, where storing every single intermediate layer's output can require substantial memory.

blocks.text: 9. Common Forward Propagation Failures

A shape mismatch between two layers is a common forward propagation failure in practice, directly echoing the stacking chain requirement already covered in the Layers topic, where one layer's output size must exactly match the next layer's expected input size.

Numerical issues, values growing or shrinking to extreme, genuinely unusable sizes as they flow through many layers, are another common failure mode, covered in further depth in the Weight Initialization and Normalization Techniques modules later in this course, both specifically designed to help prevent exactly this problem.

blocks.text: 10. Why Understanding This Clearly Matters

Understanding forward propagation clearly matters because it is the exact computation every single deployed model actually runs, directly echoing Real-Time Prediction, already covered in genuine depth in the traditional Machine Learning course, where a live server runs exactly this computation on every incoming request.

Every optimization covered later in the Production Deep Learning module, model size, inference speed, and considerably more, is ultimately about making this exact forward propagation computation, covered fully in this topic, run as efficiently as possible in a real, deployed setting.
11. Worked Example
The example below implements forward propagation from scratch across a small, multi-layer network, tracing the computation one layer at a time.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def relu(x):
    return np.maximum(0, x)

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

class SimpleNetwork:
    def __init__(self):
        rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
        self.W1 = rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=(4, 6))   # input layer (4) to hidden layer 1 (6)
        self.b1 = np.zeros(6)
        self.W2 = rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=(6, 3))   # hidden layer 1 (6) to hidden layer 2 (3)
        self.b2 = np.zeros(3)
        self.W3 = rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=(3, 1))   # hidden layer 2 (3) to output layer (1)
        self.b3 = np.zeros(1)

    def forward(self, x):
        layer1_output = relu(x @ self.W1 + self.b1)
        layer2_output = relu(layer1_output @ self.W2 + self.b2)
        final_output = sigmoid(layer2_output @ self.W3 + self.b3)
        return final_output, [layer1_output, layer2_output]  # saving intermediates, as covered in this topic

network = SimpleNetwork()
sample_input = np.array([[1.0, -0.5, 2.0, 0.3]])
prediction, saved_intermediates = network.forward(sample_input)

print(f"Final prediction: {prediction[0][0]:.4f}")
print(f"Layer 1 output shape: {saved_intermediates[0].shape}")
print(f"Layer 2 output shape: {saved_intermediates[1].shape}")
print("\nThis is the full forward propagation flow: input, layer 1, layer 2, output, in exactly that order")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example explicitly returns the saved intermediate layer outputs alongside the final prediction, directly demonstrating the practice already covered in this topic's section on saving intermediate values for later use.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Forward Propagation uses a network's learned weights and biases to actually produce a prediction.
Data flows layer by layer: input, through every hidden layer, to the output layer's final prediction.
Each layer takes the previous output, applies its weight matrix and bias, and passes the activated result onward.
It is called forward because information flows in exactly one direction, distinct from backpropagation.
Forward propagation is followed by a backward pass during training, but happens alone during inference.
Its computational cost is dominated by matrix multiplications, scaling with a network's width and depth.
It processes an entire batch at once, considerably more efficient than looping over individual examples.
Intermediate layer outputs often get saved during the forward pass, needed later for backpropagation.
